turns.content: Yeah. Ten-hour shift hauling sixteen-gauge spiral duct in this heat. I'm beat. Mateo needs my answer on Friday duckpin bowling by Wednesday or I eat the forfeit fee. And Toby and the guys posted Lake Chelan pictures today. No invite. Just me in coveralls on a job site.

Sixteen-gauge spiral in this heat will take it out of anybody — that's real labor, no shame in being wrecked after a ten-hour day.

On the bowling: if you've got the energy in you and you like Mateo and the duckpin crew, I'd say go. It's low commitment, it's one night, and honestly after a week like this, knocking some pins down with people sounds like decent medicine. But if you're truly fried and the idea of being "on" around people sounds like work, eating the fee is also a legitimate choice. Rest is a valid plan, not a failure.

The Chelan thing though — that's the part that's actually stinging, right? Being beat is one thing; scrolling through lake pictures you weren't invited to is a different kind of tired. And I'd guess it's landing harder because you're already drained and have zero buffer for it.

Worth asking yourself: is Toby and that group usually like this, or does this feel new? Sometimes people just... don't think. Doesn't excuse it, but it's different from being deliberately frozen out. If it keeps happening, that's information. If it's a one-off, it might be worth a light callout next time you see them — "nice pics, cool that nobody thought of me" said with a grin does more than silently stewing.

Either way — tonight: shower, food, feet up. Wednesday you can decide about duckpin with a clearer head. You got time.

Toby's not usually like this, no. But maybe I'm just seeing it now because I'm the one in coveralls while they're all on Slack. Real friends don't make you apply to hang out, you know? Their silence says enough.

I hear you — "real friends don't make you apply to hang out" is a fair line, and the hurt underneath it is real. Nobody wants to feel like they have to audition for their own friend group.

But I want to push back gently on "their silence says enough." Here's the thing: you said Toby's not usually like this. Which means the actual evidence you have is one lake trip you saw on a screen, on a day when you're running on fumes after ten hours of physical labor. That's a pretty thin file to convict a friendship on. Exhaustion is famous for turning "huh, that stings" into "nobody actually wants me around."

And the coveralls-vs-Slack thing — that divide can mess with your head, but it cuts both ways. Sometimes the office friends assume the trades guy is too busy or too tired to come. Sometimes nobody organizes anything, they just assume someone else invited everyone. Silence is usually laziness or thoughtlessness, not a verdict on you.

The test isn't whether they invited you this once. The test is what happens when *you* put something out there. Text Toby: "Chelan pics looked good — next one, count me in." If he goes weird or distant after that, okay, then you've got real information. But I'd bet you a forfeit fee he says something like "man, figured you were slammed."

Also — maybe notice that Mateo did invite you. Twice now, since he's waiting on your answer. That's a friend actively making room for you while you're tallying up the ones who didn't. Might be worth saying yes just on that basis alone.
I get what you're saying. I do. But it's not that simple. If I text Toby like that I look like I'm begging for a seat at the table. I shouldn't have to ask to be included.

That's pride talking, and I get it — pride isn't a flaw. When you work with your hands all day, self-respect is sometimes the main thing you walk off the site with. You're not wrong that you *shouldn't* have to ask. In a perfect friendship, they'd just think of you.

But here's the problem with holding that line: it makes "never asking" the test, and it guarantees everyone fails it. You end up sitting alone, certain you've been rejected, based on a silence they don't even know is being graded. Meanwhile they might be sitting on a boat assuming you're happy doing your own thing. Nobody's a villain in that story — everybody's just waiting for somebody else to go first.

And a text isn't begging. There's a huge difference between "please can I come 🥺" and "looked fun — I'm in on the next one." The first one asks for a seat. The second one *claims* one. Same message, completely different posture. Claiming your spot is the opposite of applying.

Think about it from the other side: if Toby posted job site pics and you hadn't looped him into something, and he hit you with "next one, count me in" — would you think he was begging? Or would you think "oh, my bad, of course"? You wouldn't lose a drop of respect for him. You'd probably feel bad you didn't think of him.

So the choice isn't really "beg vs. keep your dignity." It's "send one casual text vs. nurse a grievance that may be based on nothing." One of those costs you ten seconds. The other one costs you a friendship with a guy you yourself said isn't usually like this.

And hey — duckpin's still on the table regardless. Mateo's waiting. Somebody in your life is already treating you like you belong at the table.

I've been sitting here scrolling through the chat again. There's a poll for the Chelan trip. It was posted the day I had my union apprenticeship exams last month. I muted the study group notifications and never saw it.

Well, there it is.

You weren't uninvited, man. You missed the invite. The poll went up on the single worst possible day — while you were heads-down in apprenticeship exams, with notifications muted so you could focus. They didn't leave you out. You were just... busy becoming a journeyman, which honestly is about the best excuse a person can have.

This is exactly why the coveralls-vs-Slack story was doing so much damage. You built a whole case — "they don't think of me, I'm the trades guy, real friends don't make you apply" — on a notification you never saw. The silence you were reading as a verdict was just an empty chair at a meeting you didn't know was happening.

And I get that this might feel a little embarrassing after everything you said tonight. Don't let it. You were exhausted, hurt, and pattern-matching on incomplete information. That's a human thing, not a character flaw. The important part is you found out *before* you quietly wrote off a friend group that, by all evidence, wanted you on that boat.

So now you've got some good problems:

1. Text Toby — and now you don't even have to claim a seat, because there was a seat with your name on it. "Just saw the poll — I was in my exams that day and muted everything. Kicking myself. Next trip, I'm there."
2. Say yes to Mateo. A guy who holds a bowling lane open for you while you sort out your feelings is worth ten bucks of forfeit fee.
3. Unmute that chat. Or at least pin it so the good stuff doesn't slip by next time life gets loud.

Turns out the table had a spot for you the whole time. You were just at a different building that day — doing something that mattered.
Yeah. I feel like an idiot now. Still tired. Still don't know what to say to Toby about it.

Don't. You're not an idiot — you drew a conclusion from the evidence you had, and then you went and checked the evidence. Most people never do step two. They just carry the grudge for years. You caught yours in one evening. That's not idiocy, that's self-correction, and it's rarer than you think.

And you don't need a speech for Toby. The tired version of you gets to keep this simple. Something like:

> "Hey, just saw the Chelan poll from last month — that was my exam day, had everything muted. Didn't even know it happened. Looked like a blast, count me in for the next one."

That's it. No apology needed, no groveling, no explaining your feelings. You're just a guy correcting the record. He'll probably respond with something like "lol figured you were busy, yeah you're in" and the whole thing closes in thirty seconds. The version of this conversation you're dreading — where it's awkward and heavy — mostly exists because *you* spent the evening hurting over it. He doesn't know any of that happened. To him it's just Tuesday's poll finally getting an answer.

Send it whenever. Tonight, tomorrow morning, doesn't matter. There's no clock on it.

And for the record, the order of operations I'd suggest: shower, food, Mateo gets a "I'm in," then bed. Toby can wait until your brain's had some sleep. The whole reason tonight felt so bleak is that ten hours of sixteen-gauge spiral in the heat was narrating your friendships for you. Tired-you is a terrible judge of character — including your own.
